where: the Last name and Grade fields directly under the amber "Marcus Webb is editing this record too" notice, upper half of the sheet
finding: The round-1 lock is gone, which was right, but what replaced it does the thing J5 forbids in so many words: "whoever is second must not be typing over a value that is about to be replaced by one they cannot see." Dana opens Ava Chen while Marcus's queued change to Last name and Grade is in flight. The Last name box is prefilled "Chen" and the Grade select reads "9th grade" — the stale upstream values. The notice tells her his change exists, tells her it "goes out before anything you save", and never once tells her what he changed them to. She has no way to see "Chen-Ito" from this screen. She taps the 56px Save changes and her form posts Chen and 9th grade; her job drains after his, reads fresh, finds a difference, and patches his correction back out — in the church's permanent people database, silently, with both leaders believing they succeeded. The frame's own sentence, "Nothing here is locked — but those two boxes are about to change under you", is an accurate description of a data-loss path presented as reassurance.
evidence:
sync-editor--phone-fold and -full. Markup: Last name `` with hint `

◷ Marcus's change to this is still going out.

`; Grade `
direction: The second leader has to be able to read the value that is about to land, not just that one exists: put it in the field's own hint ("◷ Marcus is changing this to Chen-Ito, 40s ago") the way the Birthday hint already names a value. And the save that follows should carry only the fields this leader actually touched, so an untouched stale box cannot become an instruction. A lock would also solve it and is not available — round 1 established that the lock stops at the Planning Center boundary and that the owner of a queued job must not be frozen out, so the answer has to be visibility plus a narrower payload.

where: "Send mine again" and "Keep theirs" at the foot of the amber strip, roughly 460–545 CSS px down the screen, and the two comparison cells above them
finding: This is a genuine two-way decision — is the hyphen Dana's correction or the office's? — and the frame picks a side with its composition. "Send mine again" is the full-width filled brand pill, the brightest and largest object on the record, sitting where a thumb rests; "Keep theirs" is 14px underlined grey text below it. In a corridor, one-handed, the blue one is what gets tapped, and tapping it pushes Chen-Ito back over a value the church office changed deliberately four minutes ago — a write into somebody else's system, one tap, no confirmation, no undo path shown. Nothing about the screen is wrong on the facts; what is wrong is that the safe reading (leave it, the record is currently consistent) is the quiet option and the overwrite is the default.
evidence: sync-differs--phone-fold. Send mine again: `bg-brand-500 … min-h-11 w-full` = 44 × 358 CSS px, device y885–970. Keep theirs: `text-ink-400 underline … min-h-11 w-full`, 44 CSS px, separated by gap-3 + mt-1 = 16 CSS px, both spanning the full strip width. Both retire the job; neither carries a confirmation. In the comparison above, the right-hand label "PLANNING CENTER HOLDS" wraps to two lines while "YOU TYPED" does not, so the two 14px values sit at different baselines — Chen-Ito at device y790, Ito at y822, 16 CSS px apart — and neither cell is marked as the one currently on the record; only the prose says so.
direction: Give the two moves equal visual weight on touch — two secondary buttons, or the primary reserved for nothing at all here — so the screen reads as a question rather than an instruction. Align the two values on one baseline (label above, value below, both single-line) and mark the cell that is live on the record right now, so the pair can be resolved in a glance instead of a paragraph.

where: Priya Raman's "≠ Changed" chip on row six, and the "In flight 4" / "Saves failed 1" pills at roughly 420–475 CSS px
finding: The landed mark asked for in round 1 is there and the sending/waiting pair now sorts by glyph — both fixed properly. But `differs`, the state the journey brief says is most likely to be dropped, has been filed with the states that need nobody. Priya Raman's row carries `≠ Changed` in `uxr-job-run`: the same warn hue and the same dashed pill as Queued, Waiting and Sending, which are exactly the three "do nothing, it resolves itself" states. Hue is read before words on a phone, so a row that needs a human decision reads as a row that is still working. And the aggregate that was added to save the leader from scrolling does not name it: the pills say In flight 4 and Saves failed 1, and there are three visibly running rows plus Amara's pending link plus Priya's differs — so the reader cannot tell whether differs was counted as in-flight or not counted at all. Either way no number on the screen says "one record is waiting on your judgement about a value". With four rows above the fold, Priya's row six is off-screen, and the pills are the only survey a phone gets.

where: the closing clause of the queued strip: "and it goes on its own, even if you lock your phone"
finding: The concrete harm from round 1 is gone — no phone is told about a tab, and the strip now says exactly one state with a cancel affordance that is only true in that state. What remains is that the promise is unconditional and the offline case still has no words of its own. Marcus in a basement corridor, the case the brief calls ordinary, sees a strip that is pixel-identical to the one Dana sees on church wifi, and it tells him the edit proceeds without him when in fact nothing has left the handset. He is right in the end — the write does go when the app next has signal — so the cost is a temporarily false belief rather than a lost correction. Judged against the two things the ideator declined this round, this is survivable and it is not the biggest hole; the editor's stale prefill is.

Nothing has reached Planning Center yet, so you can still stop it — and it goes on its own, even if you lock your phone." The `lg:hidden` / `hidden lg:inline` pair changes only tab-versus-phone, not connected-versus-not. No frame in the round shows a device-held write, and the row chip vocabulary has no mark for one.
direction: Qualify the clause rather than build a scene: when the write has not been acknowledged by the server, the same strip reads "Held on this phone — no signal" and "It goes as soon as you have signal, even if you lock the screen", with the existing `uxr-job-mute` chip on the row. Same object, one extra branch.

where: the record-level strip across all eight scenes — the states it still has no phone render for
finding: Four of the nine states now have a phone record frame: queued (sync-profile), differs, failed, orphaned. `sending` and `waiting` exist only as 12px row chips, and `stalled` exists nowhere at any level. The declined stalled frame is survivable only if the sending strip carries an age, and no frame in this round demonstrates that it does — the one strip that prints a duration is the queued one. That matters where J3 meets the 120-second ceiling: Marcus locks his phone, the job runs four minutes, and whoever opens the record next needs "it may still land — nothing has failed", not an unaged "Sending to Planning Center" that they will read as either done or broken depending on mood.
